When you want to know how a person feels, you ask:

grammarNotes: In this lesson you’ll learn to make “requests”. “Request” quer dizer um pedido, uma forma educada de pedir algo.
To make a polite request, you use the expression “Could you...” or “Can you...”, both in formal or in informal situations. You can answer with Sure or Of course.
For example,
I’m thirsty. Could you bring me some water?
Sure.
I’m so hot. Can you open the window?
Of course.
Match the feelings and the requests.

And the answers are:
I’m cold. 		Could you close the window?
I’m hungry. 	Could you give me some food?
I’m thirsty.	Could you give me some water?
I’m hot. 		Could you open the window?
I’m sick. 		Could you pray for me? / Could you take care of me?
Now let’s practice some pronunciation. About the pronunciation of “Could you”, It’s the sound /U/, not /u/.
And the /d/ in COULD + the y in YOU become /dj/.
Listen.
It’s also important to mention that the expression Could you...? is a weak syllable. The stressed syllables in the sentence are the MAIN VERB after you and the last stressed syllables. For example,
Could you give me some water?
Could you open the window?
Listen to the phrases. Repeat them. Practice the pronunciation and the Intonation and stress.

lessons.title: Reading – Metaphors and symbols in the Bible

vocabulary: manna – maná; flesh – carne; blood – sangue
grammarNotes: In the Bible, Jesus compares himself with inanimate things. That is a metaphor, a symbol or a representation, for example, “Jesus is the door” (John 10). It is not a literal sentence, because Jesus is not really a door. It is just a symbol, a comparison.
You use a door to pass from one place to another place. With Jesus you pass from life on earth to eternal life with God, so that's why we say Jesus is a door!
The Bible has a lot of metaphors. Look at the sentences. Which verses from the book of John are food metaphors?
1. __ I am the bread of life. (6.48)
2. __ I am the light of the world. (8.12)
3. __ I am the door. (10.7)
4. __ I am the door of the sheep. (10.9)
5. __ I am the living bread which came down from heaven. (6.51)
6. __ I am the resurrection and the life. (11.25)
7. __ I am the way, the truth and the life. (14.6)
8. __ I am the true vine. (15.5)
The food metaphors are “I am the bread of life” and “I am the living bread that came down from heaven”.
Now read the passage from John 6. It says that Jesus is the bread of life. This text has some metaphors.
Pause the video and do exercises 1 to 3.

Jesus: I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the desert, but I am the living bread which comes from heaven. When you eat this bread, you have eternal life. This bread is my flesh. I give it for the life of the world.
The Jews: How can you give your flesh to eat?
Jesus: When you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you have life in you. My flesh is real food and my blood is real drink. When you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you have eternal life.
Adapted from John 6.48-56

lessons.title: Presentation, Vocabulary and Grammar Count and non-count nouns
lessons.skill: Presentation, Vocabulary and Grammar Count and non

grammarNotes: The name of this lesson is “Could you bring me a little water?”. In this lesson, you’ll learn more vocabulary about food or beverages. You’ll also learn a very important grammar concept about nouns (substantivos) – the concept of count and non-count nouns.

The Bible character in this lesson is Elijah. His story is in 1 Kings. In 1 Kings 17.10-14, Elijah visits a widow, the widow of Zarephtah. A widow is a woman who doesn’t have a husband, because he has died (ele faleceu). Do you know this story?
Look at the pictures. Read the story. Answer the questions.
Elijah and the Widow of Zarephtah
Elijah: I’m thirsty. Could you bring me a little water? Bring me, please, a little bread.
Widow: I don’t have any bread – just a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug.

Elijah: Don’t be afraid. First make some bread for me. Then make some bread for you and your son. This is what the Lord, the God of Israel says: “The jar of flour and the jug of oil will not end until there’s rain on the land!”
3.	Does the woman have any children? How many_____________________________
And the answers are:
1.	Who are the people in this story? Elijah, the widow of Zarephtah, and her son
2.	How does Elijah feel? He’s hungry and thirsty.
3.	Does the woman have any children? How many? Yes, she has one son.
Read the text again. There are four food items or beverages in the story. Find them.
The four food items in this story are:
- water (água)
- bread (pão)
- flour (farinha)
- oil (óleo)
Essa é uma linda história que descreve a provisão de Deus! Ele não deixou faltar o alimento para aquela família num momento de grande seca na terra de Israel. Ele continua fazendo o mesmo ainda hoje!
Mas voltando aos alimentos na casa da viúva:

These food items and beverages have one thing in common – they are non-count nouns. This type of noun doesn’t have a plural form. You don’t say one water, two waters, for example, or two breads, three oils, five flours. You only use these nouns in the singular form: water, bread, flour, oil.
Count nouns have a plural form, for example, bananas, avocados, apples, tomatoes. You count bananas, for example,
But with non-count nouns, to express quantity, you have to add a quantity expression.
COULD YOU GIVE ME A LITTLE WATER?
Bring me A LITTLE bread.
I only have a HANDFUL of flour
A LITTLE oil in a jug
Note that liquids and meats are non-count, but the animal is count. For example, crab and shrimp:
There are two crabs here. There are two shrimps on the plate,
but when you speak about the food, it’s non-count.
I love shrimp. / I don’t like crab.
Let’s do one more exercise. Look at the pictures of food and beverages. Are the nouns count or non-count?
And the answers are:
Count nouns: strawberry, lemon, watermelon
Non-count nouns: cabbage, milk, pork, tea, chicken
Remember: liquids are non-count! An exception is “coffee”. Informally, you can say “a coffee”. It means “a cup of coffee”.

With count nouns, you use “How many”, for example:
How many bananas?
How many tomatoes?
You use “How Much” with non-count nouns.
How much water do you drink?
How much coffee?

Now read the passage about “Money in the Bible”. Say T for True and F for False.
MONEY IN THE BIBLE

The Bible mentions money in the Old and in the New Testament. In Abraham’s time, they used metals, especially silver. In about 560 B.C. they started using metal coins made of gold, silver, bronze, and copper.
In Jesus’ time, there were five different currencies in that region:
Currency		Nationality	Material		Biblical reference
Lepton 		Jewish		copper		Mark 12.42, Luke 21.2
Dracma		Greek		silver		Matthew 17.24
Mina			Greek		silver		Luke 19.11-27
Denarius		Roman		silver		Matthew 20.1-16
Aureus (25 denarii)	Roman		gold				-
From: Enciclopedia de Biblia e Teologia

2. In Abraham’s time, they used silver coins. ____________
3. In Jesus’ time, they used bronze coins. _______
4. The dracma was a Jewish coin. _________
5. The denarius was a gold coin. _________
And the answers are:
False. In the New and in the Old Testament.
True.
False. They used copper, silver, and gold medals.
False. It was a Greek coin.
False. It was a silver coin.

Now let’s see some vocabulary about American dollars? The American dollar is the currency they use in the United States. One dollar equals 100 cents. Their American dollar coins and bills have special names:

grammarNotes: In this lesson, you’ll learn an important grammar topic for this lesson –demonstratives. You use demonstratives to point to specific objects. There are four demonstratives in English:
This 	That 	These 	Those
For example, this bottle of water is near me. It’s close to me.
That bottle of water is far from me.
These bottles of water are close to me. Those bottles of water are far from me.
So, complete:
Are this and that for singular or plural?
Are these and those for singular or plural?
Are this and these for something close to you or far from you?
Are that and those for something close to you or far from you?
THIS	    		THAT			THESE			THOSE

3 ASK ABOUT PRICE
Singular

Note about prices
4 for a dollar = 4 por um dólar
50 cents each = 50 cents cada
50 cents a pound = 50 cents a libra
Pound é a medida usada nos Estados Unidos. Eles não usam o sistema métrico, como o quilo, grama, etc. Uma libra (one pound) equivale a 483 gramas.
4. SAY WHAT YOU WANT / DIZER O QUE VOCÊ QUER
